executive_summary:
ReTargetAgent/Beam is a ~44k LOC live, auto-deploying SaaS with a healthy outer shell (good HMAC verification, react-query adoption, Alembic migrations, a real prompt-injection mitigation, blind-index PII hashing) wrapped around a decaying core. The two dominant decay themes are (1) god-files with heavy copy-paste — identity_resolver.py (1711 LOC), visitors.py (1390), api.ts (1609), twitter_browser.py (675) — and (2) a cluster of genuinely dangerous design bugs concentrated on the public/outbound surface: three SSRF holes (two unauthenticated), two cross-tenant PII leaks on the public demo path, an invite-gate-bypassing legacy signup, a hardcoded fallback HMAC key that defeats the blind index, and — most important commercially — an outbound email/CRM/alert path that will cold-email a RANDOM company employee because the 'company-level guess' classification is computed but never enforced at any send gate.

Because the repo auto-deploys to prod on every commit and the owner is non-technical and reviews each phase, the plan front-loads zero-risk, behavior-preserving wins (dead-code deletion, type-hint fixes, pure de-dup helpers) so the owner builds confidence on safe diffs, then isolates each confirmed bug into its own small, independently-verifiable phase. Migration-bearing model work and large god-file splits are deliberately pushed last and split into the smallest reviewable units. Every phase ships independently, has a concrete verification command, and avoids touching the working auth/HMAC/react-query infrastructure.

Recommended path: approve Phases 1-4 (safe cleanup) as a batch, then take the security/outbound bugfix phases (5-9) one at a time with the owner watching prod after each deploy, then schedule the restructures (10-15) only when the test suite is green and there is appetite for review-heavy diffs.
health_rationale: Score 5/10: structurally average, with real but contained risk. POSITIVES that keep it off the floor: webhook HMAC verification uses timing-safe compare_digest everywhere; auth correctly prevents RS256/HS256 algorithm confusion; react-query is adopted repo-wide with a working layout-level token gate; Alembic migrations are in place; the pixel respects most privacy signals; prompt-injection has a genuine (if imperfect) mitigation; 503 tests collect cleanly and the documented Playwright anti-patterns have been eradicated. NEGATIVES that pull it down: four 1000-1700 LOC god-files with tripled provider surfaces and verbatim copy-paste; a confirmed false-positive identity pipeline (random company employee saved as a real person) whose 'company' label is enforced at ZERO outbound gates — the single highest-severity finding; three SSRF vectors (two unauthenticated on the public /demo surface) reachable from a live prod host; two cross-tenant PII disclosures on the public demo endpoints; a hardcoded fallback HMAC key that silently defeats the blind index when misconfigured; an invite-gate-bypassing legacy signup; broken asyncpg Celery patterns that will fail the moment a worker is enabled; a re-segmentation/double-billing loop; and pervasive timezone-naive datetime columns. The decay is concentrated (you can name the ~8 files), the dead code is unusually high (dead provider wrappers, dead mock builders, dead Cloudflare worker, dead schemas), and the security surface is the kind that bites a live B2B product hard — hence a middling 5, not higher.
themes: God-files with tripled/copy-paste surfaces (identity_resolver 1711, visitors 1390, api.ts 1609, twitter_browser 675, enricher, csv_exporter)
Unenforced safety classifications: 'company-level' identity guesses and weak/timestampless matches flow unchecked into email/CRM/alert send gates
Public-surface security holes: 3x SSRF (2 unauthenticated), 2x cross-tenant PII leak on /demo, invite-gate-bypassing legacy signup, hardcoded fallback HMAC key
High dead-code load: dead provider wrappers, dead AI mock builders, dead Cloudflare worker, duplicate dependency manifests, dead schemas/fixtures
Latent concurrency/async bugs: broken asyncpg Celery loop pattern, non-atomic budget/usage check-then-increment races, re-segmentation double-billing
Timezone-naive datetime sprawl and inconsistent Base-column redeclaration across models
Silent error-swallowing and false-success UI (empty catches, false 'Copied!', false 'verified' pixel, mock-draft-on-LLM-failure persisted as real)

Keep the existing demo IP rate limit but treat it as defense-in-depth only (X-Forwarded-For is spoofable)

sequencing_rationale:
The ordering is governed by three constraints stacked in priority: (1) the repo auto-deploys to prod on every commit, so the SAFEST diffs must come first to build owner trust and de-risk the early deploys; (2) the owner is non-technical and reviews each phase, so risky work must be split into the smallest independently-shippable units with concrete verification; (3) confirmed design bugs must be fixed BEFORE the large restructures that move their code, so the bugfix tests act as a behavior-lock before decomposition.

Phases 1-4 are pure cleanup (dead-code deletion, type-hint fixes, behavior-identical de-dup, error-surfacing UX) — near-zero regression risk, high ROI, and they shrink the surface every later phase reviews against. They have almost no dependencies and can be approved as one batch.

Phases 5-12 are the bugfixes, ordered by attack-surface severity and isolation. SSRF (5) and public-surface PII/auth bypass (6) come first because they are the only findings with live unauthenticated external reach and their fixes are isolated to the public/demo/legacy surface (paying-customer flows untouched). Secrets/config hardening (7) follows because it depends on the Phase-2 type fixes and gates the encryption that PII relies on. Identity-resolution correctness (8) precedes the outbound-gate enforcement (9) because the gate (9) consumes the corrected identity_level; (9) is the single highest-commercial-severity fix (stop cold-emailing random employees) and is marked high-risk because it changes who receives email. Concurrency/async (10) and pixel/infra/deps (11) and the remaining validation/idempotency bugs (12) follow, with 12 depending on the dnspython dependency added in 11 and the retry de-dup from 3.

Phases 13-15 are the restructures, deliberately last: the router-ownership dependency (13) depends on the SSRF/PII fixes so it doesn't refactor around code that's about to change; the identity_resolver split (14) and the remaining god-file splits (15) are XL, high-review, and depend on their bugfixes being locked by tests first — splitting a file you're about to fix is how regressions hide. Each restructure's verification is explicitly 'zero behavior change, full suite + e2e green, deploy behind PR env first.'
global_risks: Auto-deploy to prod on every commit: any phase that lands is live immediately. Mitigation — use the existing PR Railway preview env (pr-64 pattern in MEMORY) for the high-risk Phases 9, 14, 15 before merging to main; owner should watch prod for 10-15 min after each bugfix deploy.

Phase 9 changes who receives outbound email/CRM/alerts. If the identity_level gate is too aggressive it could silently suppress legitimate person-level sends; if too loose it re-opens the cold-email hole. Requires explicit decision on unknown/None providers (recommend default-deny) and post-deploy verification of actual send volume.

Phase 7 secrets hardening can BLOCK prod boot if Railway lacks APP_ENV=production or ENCRYPTION_KEY. Operator must confirm those env vars are set before this phase deploys, or the app will refuse to start (by design).

Migration-bearing phases (6 composite-unique on Post, plus any model changes) run against a populated prod DB via the Dockerfile auto-`upgrade head`. The Post.platform_post_id unique swap must drop-then-add carefully and be tested on a prod clone; a bad migration on a live table is the worst-case blast radius. Note MEMORY warns of a possible multi-head from an uncommitted CRM migration — check `alembic heads` before generating new revisions.

Vercel runs `next build` (with lint) on deploy, so any TS/lint error in frontend phases (4, 15) fails the prod deploy even when test.yml CI is green — always run `npm run build` locally before merging frontend work.

Test coverage gaps mean some bugfixes lack a strong existing net: event ingestion has no positive-persistence test, the Clerk webhook and custom-domain verifier have zero active tests, and the Beam cross-site identity tests are tautological. Several phases must ADD the verifying test as part of the phase rather than relying on existing coverage.

The two divergent requirements.txt manifests (Phase 11) mean a dependency that imports fine locally may be absent from the prod Docker image; reconcile and verify in a clean venv before relying on any new dep (dnspython for Phase 12 MX fix specifically).

Effort is back-loaded: Phases 14-15 are XL god-file splits on a live UI/router. They carry real regression risk and low immediate ROI, so they should only be scheduled when the suite is green and there is explicit appetite — it is legitimate to ship Phases 1-13 and defer 14-15 indefinitely.
